title: SYSK Selects: Is there such a thing as a truth serum?
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the April 2013 episode on truth serums. Josh introduces it as a selection and explains it was prompted by the James Holmes (Aurora, Colorado theater shooter) case, in which a judge approved narco analysis testing. The hosts cover the history of so-called truth serums: scopolamine and the Dallas obstetrician Dr. House's "twilight sleep" experiments, the side effects of scopolamine, the Colombian drug-gang legend, Lovenhart's accidental discovery with barbiturates, Muhlberger's use in Michigan, the 1940s Fort Dix malingerer study by Gerson and Victor Off (sodium amytal), barbiturate dosing stages, and the problems of false or manipulated confessions and admissibility in court. They also discuss amphetamines (Benzedrine and Methedrine), psychiatrist J.M. McDonald's skepticism, and a declassified CIA white paper "Truth Drugs and Interrogation" by George Morrell (transcribed as Memorrell/Bimmerell). The episode closes with a shout-out to horror writer Melissa Maninny and a listener email about Aaron's grandfather Ron Brown, an animal actor and trainer for Disney.

entities.name: Truth, Drugs and Interrogation (CIA white paper)

segments.title: Selects intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces this Selects episode, originally aired April 2013, and explains the James Holmes case and a judge's approval of narco analysis testing prompted the topic.

segments.title: Defining truth serums and narco analysis vs. narco interrogation
segments.summary: The hosts explain that truth serums do not necessarily produce truth, that LSD is not a truth drug, and distinguish narco analysis (psychological truth) from narco interrogation (revealing crimes).

segments.title: Scopolamine and Dr. House's experiments
segments.summary: A Dallas obstetrician, Dr. House, used chloroform, morphine and scopolamine on laboring women, found them candid, and proposed using it on criminals. William Moulton Marston's early scopolamine study is also mentioned.

segments.title: Scopolamine side effects and the threat of injection
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the unpleasant side effects of scopolamine, including dry mouth, hallucinations and headaches, why it fell out of use, and the Colombian drug-gang dosing legend.

segments.title: Barbiturates discovered by accident
segments.summary: Arthur Lovenhart at the University of Wisconsin accidentally found a catatonic patient became talkative after an injection, leading to barbiturate use; Clarence Muhlberger in Michigan followed up. Common barbiturates and nicknames are listed.

segments.title: Fort Dix malingerer study and court admissibility
segments.summary: Gerson and Victor Off used sodium amytal on suspected malingering soldiers at Fort Dix. The hosts discuss George Morrell's commentary on setting and rapport, and courts' reluctance to admit drug-induced confessions, including a New Jersey case.

segments.title: Barbiturate stages, risks and manipulation
segments.summary: The hosts describe the stages of barbiturate sedation, the risk of death, delirium and false memories, and how interrogators could manipulate subjects while they were groggy. They note a skilled interrogator might get the same information without drugs.

segments.title: Amphetamines, psychiatrist skepticism and self-possessed subjects
segments.summary: Benzedrine and Methedrine were tried because they might make subjects talk quickly. Psychiatrist J.M. McDonald is skeptical of confessions, noting self-possessed subjects can resist and neurotic subjects may be more likely to confess.

segments.title: CIA white paper on truth drugs
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a declassified CIA white paper by George Morrell on truth drugs, its uses such as detecting feigned language ability, Soviet use, and training agents by dosing them.

segments.title: Shout-out, listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: Shout-out to horror writer Melissa Maninny, a listener email about Aaron's grandfather Ron Brown, a Disney animal actor and trainer, and the closing sign-off.
